A score you can take apart

MTDI Studio · October 2026

Confidence numbers usually arrive as a single percentage with nothing behind it. MTDI's score is built the other way round: eight named factors, each computed from something measurable, each with a visible weight. If the score is 71 %, you can see which factor cost what.

The eight factors

FactorWeightMeasured from
Availability0.20Is the channel connected and fresh?
Baseline0.15Has Environmental Intelligence finished learning?
Signal to noise0.20How clearly a change stands above the measured ambient noise
Clipping0.15Is the raw value inside its declared range?
Timing0.10How regular the arrival intervals are
Transient behaviour0.10Is the channel bursty, or stable/continuous?
Axial consensus0.05Do a vector's axes agree on the shape of a change?
Correlation0.05Do channels that changed together correlate?

Each factor lies between 0 and 1. A channel's score is the weighted sum, and the project's score is the mean over every declared channel. An offline channel scores zero, so a missing sensor lowers the score instead of quietly disappearing from it. Channels marked optional are left out while offline.

Two regimes for signal to noise

When a signal is present, the factor is the logarithm of the signal-to-noise ratio. At rest there is nothing to stand above the noise, so the channel is judged on resolution instead: how far its measured noise sits below the budget a healthy sensor should meet. Resolution earns at most half the credit, because a quiet channel proves a clean signal path, not a working one.

What it is not

It is a heuristic evidence-quality score, not a calibrated probability. It cannot tell you the reading is correct, only how much evidence there is that the measurement process is healthy. MTDI labels it that way everywhere it appears.

Changing the weights

A project can re-weight the factors in its manifest. For example, a project whose channels arrive irregularly by design can lower timing. Weights are renormalised to sum to one, and the interface always shows the weights in use.
